Product Details

User Rating:

Rating: 3.2
Rate This Product

2015 Bowman Chrome Baseball continues from where 2015 Bowman Baseball left off, delving into more prospects, autographs and Refractors. Like last year, hobby boxes come with a pair of signed cards rather than the one usually found in regular Bowman and Draft.

The base set has 200 rookie and veteran players done on chromium card stock. Numbered parallels include Refractors, Purple Refractors, Blue Refractors, Green Refractors, Gold Refractors, hobby-only Orange Refractors (#/25), Red Refractors (#/5) and Superfractors (1/1).

Complimenting the base set are 100 Prospects inserts of prospects and international standouts who weren't in 2015 Bowman. Both these and the Chrome Prospect Autographs come with several Refractor parallels. The colors are similar to those from the base set. Randomly inserted hot packs come with exclusive Wave Refractors parallels. Chrome Prospect Autographs come with on-card signatures.

Rookie Autographs are also hard-signed. These come from players who have already made their MLB debuts. And, yes, these have Refractors as well.

New Prime Position Autographs offer signatures from a top prospect at each position. They're signed on-card and have several numbered Refractor parallel versions.

Other signed cards in 2015 Bowman Chrome Baseball include Dual Autographs (#/25), Bowman Black Autographs and more cards from high school events like the Perfect Game Classic.

Although the Superfractor has become a hobby benchmark for one-of-a-kind cards, they're still relatively new. Superfractors That Never Were recreate past Bowman cards of current and retired players as both regular and autographed one-of-one Superfractors.

Series Next Die-Cuts is a new basic insert that spotlights MLB's youth movement. These get new parallel patterns called Haze Refractors, Vapor Refractors (#/25) and Torrent Refractors (#/5). There are also Superfractors (1/1) and Autograph versions.

Prospect Profiles Minis bring a shrunken element to 2015 Bowman Chrome Baseball. In addition to basic versions, there are numbered Refractors in the colors Green, Gold, Orange (#/25), Red (#/5) and Superfractor (1/1).

Product Configuration: Hobby - 18 packs per box, 4 cards per pack (2 base, 2 Prospects); Jumbo - 12 pack per box, 13 cards per pack (7 base, 6 Prospects)
Price Point: Low- to Mid-End Baseball Card
Target Audience: Prospectors, Autograph Collectors, Chromies

Product Review

2015 Bowman Chrome Baseball Product Review

Reviewed by Trey Treutel

Good: Two autographs per box, on-card signatures, Carlos Correa rookie cards.

Bad: Very little to set it apart, weak autograph checklist, limited color by the box.

The Bottom Line: Basically an update to 2015 Bowman, the draw here is not quite as strong for prospect collectors as most of the top names have already been covered in prior products and the recent draft picks are not present. That makes it more reliant on the rookies, which is fine, but there are plenty of other options that do the same thing and also offer bigger hit opportunities.

Staff Rating:
2.8 / 5.0

Card Design: 3.25/5.0

The 2015 Bowman base design has a solid look and it looks even better in Chrome. Like most Chrome-based products, since it simply takes a prior set and adds chromium, most collectors have already made up their minds about the design. Having said that, Chrome is synonymous with Refractors. I expected more color and better variety in the Refractor options and it seemed very subdued.

2014 Bowman Chrome gave us a few different inserts, like Fire Die-Cuts, that felt fresh. In 2015, there is really nothing of note in the boxes outside of the on-card autographs. Limited to one regular insert, one die-cut insert and one mini insert, the overall designs comes across as very generic.

I will say that the Superfractors That Never Were is a cool idea. But since 99.999999999% of collectors will never get close to pulling one, it is hard to treat that as an actual selling point.

Checklist: 2.0/5.0

The 2015 Bowman Chrome Baseball base set catches up on the rookie names, so options like Correa, Buxton, Gallo and Kang are available in addition to Kris Bryant. Still, without the rookies that are apparently being saved for 2016, it feels like the gaps are even larger.

As far as the prospects, that has always been something that takes time. Because of when the release falls in the year, the opportunities for the first options for the bigger names are slim. It is worth noting that collectors can find the 2014 prospect autograph for Michael Conforto in this release. While not all collectors liked how it was handled, it is a notable card as his first and it is better to find it here than not at all.

The Rookie Autographs are another big element where the checklist factors heavily. Given the base options, most of the top names are covered as autographs in the main rookie set. One big omission is Carlos Correa. Having recently signed him to an exclusive, I would have assumed Topps would have made a big push to get his signed rookies in this product. His autograph is only available in one insert set.

Value: 3.0/5.0

A late-season prospect product that is also geared to rookies (but the late rookie call-ups are not available) is not something that screams value. At around $60-65 a box, prices are not bad and there is always the chance that some obscure prospect blows up, but the Chrome factor is not enough to greatly enhance the value on its own.

On-card autographs always help value, but a big part of that is the checklist. Without many new or surging names, the lack of apparent value makes it a much tougher sell.

Refractors can certainly boost value, but they are just not as common in 2015 Bowman Chrome. Yeah, parallels have jumped the shark in most products, but Chrome products are the one place where collectors expect to find them and I feel it comes up way short.

The Fun Factor: 3.0/5.0

As someone who does not normally delve into the prospect world, the Bowman fun factor is not as great, but I do love some Chrome. For me, I tend to look at the things that make a product unique. On-card autographs are still uncommon enough to stand out. Other than that and the normal allure of Chrome, I just didn’t really find much that caught my attention and that was amplified by the lack of color in a product that is normally associated with it.


The box used for this review was provided by Topps.
